summary: AI-Scientist sends LLM traffic through three channels: the SDK clients built in ai_scientist/llm.py:create_client (idea generation, novelty check, reflections, paper review), two inline openai.OpenAI() clients that launch_scientist.py and experimental/launch_oe_scientist.py hand to perform_review, and aider, which drives the experiment and write-up loops through LiteLLM. I vendored router_runtime.py and wrapped all of them (plus the two clients in review_iclr_bench/iclr_analysis.py), and installed the LiteLLM hook at ai_scientist.llm import time so aider's OpenAI-provider calls route too; nothing changes until RAMP_ROUTER_API_KEY is set. Two things then blocked most of the traffic, so each got its own undoable commit: Router's Responses API rejects `seed` (every gpt/o1/o3 call in llm.py sends seed=0), and the app's default model (claude-3-5-sonnet-20240620) and hard-coded reviewer snapshot (gpt-4o-2024-05-13) are not in Router's catalog. router.policy.json now drops `seed` and maps those ids to claude-sonnet-5 and gpt-4o on Router-bound requests only. What still stays on vendor keys, deliberately: the five-way reviewer ensemble (Router has no `n`), the DeepSeek/OpenRouter/Gemini OpenAI-compatible clients (third-party hosts, models absent from the catalog), the Bedrock and Vertex Anthropic clients, and aider whenever it runs on a Claude model, which is the default and the single largest spender in the pipeline.
reviewed: I looked at where this pipeline actually spends: long repeated prompts (the reviewer re-sends the whole paper for five reflection rounds and a five-way ensemble), the one workload Router cannot serve as written (n-way sampling), unattended multi-hour runs with no fallback when a provider wobbles, spend attribution across four pipeline stages that all bill to one key, and the hard-coded reviewer model. Two improvements are built and tested on branches; four are proposals, because they change which model answers (reviewer model, fallbacks) or need a decision about aider's provider that is not mine to make.

items.title: Route every LLM client, including aider's, through Router
items.summary: Vendor router_runtime.py, wrap the Anthropic and OpenAI clients the app builds, and install the LiteLLM hook so aider's OpenAI-provider calls route too.
items.gains: One Router key in front of every channel the app uses, per-request spend and provider metadata, and the policy levers below. Nothing happens until RAMP_ROUTER_API_KEY is set, and ROUTER_MIGRATE_DISABLE=1 turns it off again.
items.why: The scanner saw nine call sites but only one client construction it could link them to: every call takes `client` as an argument. create_client is the one factory, so wrapping there covers idea generation, novelty checks, reflections and review; the two launchers also build their own openai.OpenAI() for the reviewer, so those are wrapped in place. aider never touches those clients: it builds models through LiteLLM, so the runtime's LiteLLM hook runs at ai_scientist.llm import time, which every entry point imports before it creates a Coder.

evidence.detail: 10 passed (compileall of ai_scientist, launch_scientist.py, experimental, review_iclr_bench + 6 module imports), same as baseline

check --run of a driver through create_client/get_response_from_llm: requests for gpt-4o, gpt-4o-mini and o3-mini reached router-sim as /v1/responses; a litellm.completion on gpt-4o-mini reached it too
`check --run --live` reported 'no migration key'; no live Router call was made from this session

items.title: Drop seed on Router-bound requests
items.summary: router.policy.json drops `seed` so the gpt/o1/o3 calls in llm.py can be translated to Responses.
items.gains: Every OpenAI-model call in get_response_from_llm reaches Router; before this, all of them stayed on the OpenAI key.
items.loses: OpenAI's best-effort seed determinism on routed requests. The app sets seed=0 while sampling at temperature 0.75 (temperature 1 on o1/o3) and never reads system_fingerprint, so runs were not reproducible before either, but the nominal knob is gone on the Router path.
items.price: no change per token; more traffic now priced from Router's catalog instead of OpenAI's list
items.why: Router's /v1/responses rejects `seed` with a 400, and the runtime will not silently translate a request it cannot represent, so it kept all of them on the provider. Dropping the parameter in policy applies only to Router-bound requests: if the runtime falls back to OpenAI, the original request including seed is what goes out.

evidence.detail: before: 'provider (runtime kept it) ... untranslatable: seed' for gpt-4o-mini, gpt-4o and o3-mini; after: three valid /v1/responses requests at router-sim
10 passed, unchanged

items.title: Map retired model ids to Router catalog models
items.summary: claude-3-5-sonnet-20240620/20241022 are served by claude-sonnet-5 and gpt-4o-2024-05-13 by gpt-4o on Router-bound requests.
items.gains: The app's default model and its hard-coded reviewer snapshot reach Router instead of the vendor keys. Claude Sonnet 5 is $2/$10 per 1M against Claude 3.5 Sonnet's $3/$15, so the default path also gets cheaper.
items.loses: Those runs are answered by newer models. Ideas, reviews and write-ups will differ from archived Claude 3.5 Sonnet and gpt-4o-2024-05-13 runs, and perform_review's scoring was calibrated against gpt-4o-2024-05-13, so review numbers are no longer comparable with the published ones. Undo this commit to keep the old ids on the vendor keys.
items.price: claude-sonnet-5 $2/$10 per 1M vs Claude 3.5 Sonnet $3/$15; gpt-4o unchanged at list
items.why: Router's catalog has no 2024 Claude 3.5 Sonnet and no gpt-4o-2024-05-13 snapshot, and an unknown id is a 404, so the runtime kept both on the provider. Those two ids carry almost all of this app's traffic: claude-3-5-sonnet-20240620 is the --model default and gpt-4o-2024-05-13 is hard-coded for every paper review. Without the map the migration would have moved the rarely used paths and left the default run untouched. The map lives in policy, so the provider fallback path still sends the original id.

evidence.detail: through the app's own client: 'gpt-4o-2024-05-13' reached router-sim as model=gpt-4o on /v1/responses, and 'claude-3-5-sonnet-20240620' as model=claude-sonnet-5 on /v1/messages (response reported served model claude-sonnet-5)
live catalog via `router-migrate levers`: claude-sonnet-5 in $2 / out $10 per 1M
10 passed, unchanged

items.title: Llama 3.1 405B keeps going to OpenRouter
items.summary: There is no Llama in Router's catalog, so the --model llama3.1-405b path still uses the OpenRouter key.
items.why: The catalog has open-weight ids (DeepSeek, GLM, Kimi, MiniMax, Qwen, Nemotron, gpt-oss) but no Llama, and the client points at openrouter.ai, which the runtime does not route without an explicit unlock. Mapping it onto another open-weight model would silently change which model answers, which is a decision for a human, not a default.

evidence.detail: check --run: openrouter.ai:443 appears under traffic that stays on the provider

items.title: DeepSeek and Gemini clients keep their own keys
items.summary: Those clients point at api.deepseek.com and Google's OpenAI-compatible host with model ids Router's catalog does not have.
items.why: Two things would have to be true at once: the runtime would need `unlock_hosts` for the vendor host, and the model id would have to be a catalog id. deepseek-chat/coder/reasoner and gemini-1.5/2.0 are not in the catalog (Router carries deepseek-v4* and Vertex Gemini 2.5+), and the Vertex Gemini ids need a caller-owned Google key on the Router account. Both are mappings a human should choose; see i3's sibling proposal i5.

evidence.detail: check --run: api.deepseek.com:443 and generativelanguage.googleapis.com:443 appear under traffic that stays on the provider

items.title: Bedrock and Vertex Anthropic clients stay with their cloud
items.summary: AnthropicBedrock and AnthropicVertex clients are left alone by the runtime by design.
items.why: Those clients carry AWS and GCP credentials and region routing that Router does not stand in for; the runtime explicitly keeps them on their configured endpoint. Router does list Bedrock Claude ids, but they require the caller's own provider key, so moving them is a provider-credentials decision rather than a code change.

evidence.detail: router_runtime.wrap_anthropic returns Bedrock/Vertex clients unchanged (runtime source)

items.title: The five-way reviewer ensemble stays on OpenAI
items.summary: get_batch_responses_from_llm asks for n=5 samples in one request, and Router has no `n`.
items.loses: nothing today: the ensemble still runs exactly as before, on the OpenAI key
items.why: Router's Responses API rejects `n`, so the runtime keeps the request on OpenAI. Dropping `n` would silently turn a five-sample ensemble into one sample and quietly change every review score, which is not an acceptable default. Improvement i2 asks for the five samples one at a time instead, which routes without changing how many samples the reviewer gets.

evidence.detail: check --run: 'provider (runtime kept it) ... untranslatable: seed,n' for get_batch_responses_from_llm

items.title: aider on Claude is still off Router
items.summary: The LiteLLM hook routes aider's OpenAI-provider calls, but with the default Claude model aider talks to Anthropic directly.
items.gains: nothing yet; this is the open question
items.price: unchanged: aider keeps billing the Anthropic key on the default model
items.why: aider drives the experiment loop and the whole LaTeX write-up, so it is the largest spender in a run, and the --model default is claude-3-5-sonnet-20240620. The runtime's LiteLLM hook works by installing an HTTP session that LiteLLM's OpenAI provider uses; LiteLLM's Anthropic provider does not use it, so those calls leave on the Anthropic key. Three ways out, each a real decision: run aider on an OpenAI-provider catalog model (gpt-5.3-codex or gpt-5.4-mini) and accept different code-editing behaviour; point aider at Router as an OpenAI-compatible endpoint with its own base URL, which loses per-request provider fallback; or leave aider on Anthropic and accept that Router sees only part of the spend. I did not pick one because it changes which model writes the experiments.

evidence.detail: check --run of litellm.completion after the hook: gpt-4o-mini reached router-sim as /v1/responses; claude-3-5-sonnet-20240620 went to api.anthropic.com (shown as blocked, i.e. not Router)

items.title: Cache the repeated review and reflection prompts
items.summary: Set prompt_cache_key to the feature label on Router-bound Responses requests so the reviewer's repeated paper-sized prompt is read from cache.
items.gains: The reviewer sends the same rubric plus the whole paper again for each of five reflection rounds, and perform_writeup replays a growing history per section. Router measured a 9,020-token prompt caching 8,832 tokens on the second call, with the call's cost dropping from $0.00135 to $0.00069. On gpt-4o the cached read is $1.25 against $2.50 per 1M input tokens.
items.loses: Nothing functional: it is one policy field and the prompt is unchanged. The saving is real only where a run reuses an identical prefix above about 1,024 tokens, so short idea-generation calls see nothing, and the Claude path over /v1/messages is unaffected because policy's cache key applies to Responses only.
items.price: cached input tokens bill at the catalog cache_read rate, roughly half for gpt-4o and a tenth for Claude over Responses
items.why: This is the cheapest win in the repository: a one-line policy change, no code touched, and it hits the single biggest prompt in the pipeline.

evidence.detail: router_runtime._apply_policy on a sample body adds prompt_cache_key='ai_scientist/llm.py:get_response_from_llm'; check --run still shows all requests valid at router-sim
10 passed on the branch
no migration key in this session; the cache saving is quoted from ROUTER.md's measurement, not measured here

items.title: Sample the review ensemble one request at a time
items.summary: Replace the n=5 OpenAI request in get_batch_responses_from_llm with five single requests, which is what the function already does for every other model, so the ensemble routes.
items.gains: The reviewer ensemble is the one workload Router could not serve; after this it routes like everything else, with the same number of samples, and picks up caching, fallbacks and Router's spend record.
items.loses: The prompt is billed once per sample instead of once per request: about four extra paper-sized prompts per ensemble, which prompt caching (i1) largely recovers. The five samples also run in sequence rather than server-side, so that one step takes roughly five times as long; this is a background batch pipeline, so that is wall-clock, not user-facing latency.
items.price: about +$0.05 per review ensemble at gpt-4o list prices without caching, less with i1
items.why: Reviews are where the pipeline's judgement comes from and the ensemble is five of the longest prompts it sends. Leaving it on a vendor key means Router's spend view is missing the most expensive review step, and it cannot take a fallback if OpenAI rate-limits an overnight run.

evidence.detail: check --run: get_batch_responses_from_llm now produces one valid /v1/responses request per sample at router-sim instead of 'provider (runtime kept it) ... untranslatable: seed,n'; the driver still got 2 of 2 requested responses
10 passed on the branch

items.title: Give unattended runs a fallback model
items.summary: Add a fallbacks list and a provider_timeout in router.policy.json so a rate-limited or stalled provider does not kill a multi-hour run.
items.gains: A run processes ideas for hours unattended and a failed stage aborts the whole idea (do_idea returns False). Router can try a second catalog model on the same request instead, and a provider_timeout turns a hung provider into a fast failure rather than a stalled worker.
items.loses: When the fallback fires, a different model answers and nothing in the response says which candidate failed, so a run's output can silently mix models; the reviewer's calibration assumes one model. A provider_timeout that is too tight turns slow-but-fine calls into 504s, and truncated attempts are still billed.
items.price: the serving candidate's catalog price, only when it serves
items.why: I did not apply this as part of the migration because picking the second model is a quality decision for whoever owns the research output, and because the measured fallback behaviour (silent, and no fallback once a stream has started) deserves an explicit yes. It is a policy-only change: fallbacks and provider_timeout per feature label, no code.

evidence.detail: proposal; ROUTER.md records fallbacks as measured for missing models, 403s and invalid parameters, and as not measured against real provider outages

items.title: Label spend by pipeline stage
items.summary: Add metadata (product, team) in router.policy.json so Router's spend view separates idea generation, write-up and review.
items.gains: The runtime already tags each request with its calling function as metadata.feature; adding a product and team label puts this app's spend in Ramp's spend management alongside everything else, and makes 'what does one paper cost' answerable per stage without instrumenting the code.
items.loses: Nothing functional. Messages-surface traffic (the Claude path) carries the label only as a header, and whether Router's spend views read that header is not measured, so Claude-run attribution may stay coarse.
items.why: This pipeline's whole economics question is cost per generated paper. The labels are free and the data is otherwise unrecoverable after the fact. I left it as a proposal only because the right product and team strings belong to whoever owns the Router account.

evidence.detail: proposal; ROUTER.md documents up to 16 metadata labels per request on Responses and the special user/product keys

items.title: Make the reviewer model a flag, not a constant
items.summary: Replace the hard-coded gpt-4o-2024-05-13 in both launchers with a --reviewer-model flag so the reviewer can move to a cheaper or newer catalog model.
items.gains: Review is five reflection rounds plus a five-way ensemble over a full paper, so it is the most prompt-heavy stage. gpt-4o costs $2.50/$10 per 1M; gpt-5-mini is $0.25/$2 and claude-haiku-5-5 is $0.10/$0.50. On this traffic that is an order of magnitude, and with a flag it becomes a per-run choice instead of a code edit.
items.loses: Review scores shift. perform_review's few-shot examples and thresholds were tuned against gpt-4o-2024-05-13, and no offline check here measures review quality, so changing the default would invalidate comparisons with published AI-Scientist numbers. The honest version of this change keeps gpt-4o as the default and lets a run opt into a cheaper model.
items.price: up to about -90% on review tokens if a run opts into claude-haiku-5-5; no change at the default
items.why: Hard-coding a dated model id in two launchers is what forced the t2 mapping in the first place. A flag removes that class of problem and lets the team price-tune the most expensive stage without touching code. I did not build it because it adds a user-facing CLI option, which is a product decision.

evidence.detail: live catalog via `router-migrate levers`: gpt-5-mini $0.25/$2, claude-haiku-5-5 $0.10/$0.50 per 1M

items.title: No live Router call was made
items.summary: `check --run --live` reported 'no migration key', so every routing result here comes from the local Router simulator.
items.why: The simulator enforces Router's request rules and shows which requests would reach it, which is what the routing claims above rest on. Prices and catalog membership come from the live catalog (`router-migrate levers` fetched it at 2026-10-14 21:03). Nothing here has been confirmed against the real api.router.com from this session.

evidence.detail: `router-migrate check --run CMD --live` -> 'error: no migration key'

items.title: This sandbox's Anthropic SDK rejects temperature
items.summary: anthropic 1.13.0 in the test environment raises TypeError on messages.create(temperature=...), which is how get_response_from_llm calls it.
items.why: This is pre-existing and unrelated to the migration: it reproduces on the base commit with an unwrapped client. It means the Claude branch of get_response_from_llm cannot be exercised end to end here, so t2's Claude mapping was proved through the app's own wrapped client calling messages.create without temperature, which exercises the same client, model id and surface. Worth knowing before anyone reads a Claude-path failure in this environment as a Router problem.

evidence.detail: anthropic.Anthropic().messages.create(..., temperature=0.5) raises TypeError on the base commit, no runtime involved
